title: The Good Samaritan
hookLine: the man who stopped for the wounded traveler was the one nobody expected (Luke 10:25–37)

lines: A NAME ON HOSPITALS AND LAWS.
A WEEK OF TORCHES AND ARROWS.
cards: Here's a story so well-known its name became an everyday word. Hospitals are named after it. There are laws named after it.
And the person it's named for was the one nobody listening expected to be the hero.
It ends a week of torches and arrows: Rabia's bucket, hands on an elephant in the dark, Abba Moses's leaking basket, fingers like lamps, a mother's mustard seed, an arrow that needed pulling.
Sufi, Christian and Buddhist homes, each story kept by its own people.

teach.b: It's in the Gospel of Luke, chapter ten. An expert in the Jewish law asks Jesus what he must do to inherit eternal life.

Jesus asks what the law says, and the lawyer answers with two commandments joined together: love God, and love your neighbor as yourself. Then he asks, as the King James puts it, "And who is my neighbour?"
Jesus answers with a story. A man is going down the steep road from Jerusalem to Jericho. Robbers strip him, beat him, and leave him half dead.
A priest sees him and "passed by on the other side." A Levite, a temple assistant, does the same. The text never says why.
Then a Samaritan comes. Samaritans and Jews in that time had centuries of bad blood; each side had reasons to distrust the other.

This Samaritan stops. He bandages the wounds, pouring on oil and wine, puts the man on his own animal, takes him to an inn, and pays the innkeeper two coins: whatever more it costs, I'll repay you when I come back.
Then Jesus turns the question around.
Not who counts as my neighbor, but which of these three acted like a neighbor? The lawyer answers: the one who showed him mercy.
Jesus says, "Go, and do thou likewise." This is a Jewish teacher telling a Jewish lawyer a story built on the Jewish commandment to love your neighbor. It isn't a case against priests or Levites.
Its surprise is that the helper came from the people the listeners least expected, and that being a neighbor is something you do, not something you're owed.

how: Christians read the Good Samaritan as Jesus's teaching on loving your neighbor, and churches, hospitals and charities around the world take the name for work that helps strangers in need.

games.q: you're the Samaritan on the Jericho road. a stranger lies beaten and half dead, from a people yours distrusts. what do you do?
o: pass by on the other side
bandage him, carry him to an inn, and pay
go and report it in the next town
games.why: he pours oil and wine on the wounds, carries him on his own animal to an inn, pays two coins, and promises to cover the rest.

practice: Think about the roads you'll travel today, real or online: the hallway, the bus, the checkout line, the family group chat.
Picture one place where it would be easy to pass by on the other side, and picture stopping instead: not a grand rescue, a door held, a question asked, a few minutes given.
Notice what makes stopping hard, busyness, awkwardness, and let it be there.

wordCard.voice: Samaritan. The traveler nobody expected, who stopped, bandaged, carried and paid, and turned who's my neighbor into what does a neighbor do.

orig.note: Greek: neighbor, literally the one near. the word in the lawyer's question in Luke.

carryVoice: Your line: go and do likewise. A neighbor is someone you become. Seventy-seven days, and a week of stories.
